title: Paper Rings
description: Swift's fizzy wedding-band daydream from Lover — she likes shiny things, but she'd marry him with paper rings, in a retro pop rush co-built with Jack Antonoff.

pops.text: Track eight on Lover, Swift's seventh studio album, released August 23, 2019. It was her first album for Republic Records after leaving Big Machine.
Swift wrote and produced it with Jack Antonoff. At a Lover secret session she said the template was imagining herself as a wedding band at a reception, playing the couple's love songs in about 1978.
You can hear Antonoff counting in the chorus — Swift kept the count-in on purpose, because that is how much the two of them wanted it to sound like a real wedding band.
The sound is a deliberate throwback collage: pop-punk, bubblegum, new wave, power pop and rockabilly, with tambourine jingles, bright electric guitars and girl-group-style backing vocals.
Antonoff did almost everything alongside her: programming, drums, bass, acoustic and electric guitar, keyboards, piano, percussion and background vocals. Both writers also played percussion.
It was recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York City and Metropolis Studios in London, mixed by Serban Ghenea and mastered by Randy Merrill.
The lyric is a commitment song with the price tag removed: she loves shiny things, but the vow matters more than the ring — a homemade paper ring would do.
The verses retrace the couple's history, from internet-stalking the crush and a cat-and-mouse beginning to jumping into an icy outdoor pool together in winter.
It was never released as a single, but it still debuted at its peak of No. 45 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the week Lover flooded the chart.

Fans waited years to hear it live: Swift first performed it on the Eras Tour on June 23, 2023 in Minneapolis, as a solo guitar surprise song. A Paris live recording later appeared as a bonus track on the 2025 deluxe Lover (Live from Paris).

title: Rift
description: The title track of Phish's dream-logic concept album — a man sleeps, dreams his relationship is cracking, and wakes into a taut, tricky Anastasio-Marshall opener.

pops.text: The opening and title track of Rift, Phish's fourth studio album, released February 2, 1993 on Elektra Records.
The album is a concept record about one night in a man's sleep cycle, as he dreams about the rift in his relationship with his girlfriend — and this song states the theme outright.
Trey Anastasio wrote the music and Tom Marshall the lyrics, their partnership behind most of the album. Anastasio and keyboardist Page McConnell share the lead vocals here.
The song was built in pieces between 1987 and 1992: its melody grew out of the instrumental 'With' section of 'The Curtain With,' which Phish played live in 1987 and 1988.
After that early life, 'Rift' was shelved, then reintroduced in 1992 in the form heard on the album — faster, with slightly reworked lyrics.
The album was recorded in September and October 1992 at White Crow Studios in Burlington, Vermont, on 24-track tape, with Muscle Shoals producer Barry Beckett producing.
Mixing and overdubs moved to Castle Recording Studios in Franklin, Tennessee — band photos from those sessions show Phish outside the historic studio. Bob Ludwig mastered the record.
At 6:13, the track is a precision exercise: interlocking composed sections and a guitar line that has to be played exactly right, with no room to coast.

David Welker's cover painting is a puzzle box for this album: he worked with the band to depict every track but one — 'The Horse' — somewhere in that blue bedroom scene. Relix later named it one of the most iconic album covers ever.

The album was certified gold by the RIAA on October 15, 1997, and 'Rift' itself stayed a live staple — it even opened Phish's Sphere run talk in 2026 coverage paired with Welker's artwork on the big screen.

title: Belong
description: Out of Time's strangest, loveliest moment: Michael Stipe whispers a story into a Walkman in a garage while the band answers with a wordless, soaring chorus.

pops.text: Track seven on Out of Time, R.E.M.'s seventh studio album, released in March 1991 — the record that took a cult college band to No. 1 in both the US and UK.
Right after the sugar rush of 'Shiny Happy People,' the album turns: 'Belong' opens the Memory Side with a spoken-word verse instead of a sung one.
Stipe's vocal was not recorded in the studio. He thought the studio takes were too clear, so he borrowed producer Scott Litt's Walkman and recorded it in the garage of a rental home.
He later described the three-car garage's acoustics — and a large tank of unidentified gas sitting in it — as giving the take the ambient, reverberant feel he wanted.

The spoken verses tell a small, mysterious story: a woman gets up from the kitchen table, folds the newspaper, silences the radio, and hears that creatures have jumped the barricades and headed for the sea.
Stipe explained the scene as a distant event suddenly mattering close to home: she opens the window, breathes at the thought of freedom, and whispers one word to her child — 'belong.'
The choruses have no words at all. Stipe, Mike Mills and Bill Berry layer long 'ooh' harmonies while Peter Buck's guitar jangles over a big Mills bass hook.
Listen to the drums: Berry rides the hi-hat while the kick and snare beats are reinforced with alternating finger snaps and handclaps.

The technique had an in-joke ancestor — 'Voice of Harold,' an earlier outtake where Stipe read gospel album liner notes over the '7 Chinese Bros.' backing track. 'Belong' plays the same trick completely straight.

Like all R.E.M. songs of the era, it is credited equally to Berry, Buck, Mills and Stipe. The band famously did not tour Out of Time; the 25th-anniversary edition later added a 'Belong' demo and a live Mountain Stage performance.

title: Street Fighting Man
description: 1968 bottled: a protest anthem that sounds like a wall of electric guitars but was mostly an acoustic guitar being strangled through a cheap Philips cassette recorder.

pops.text: Written by Mick Jagger and Keith Richards for Beggars Banquet, the Stones' 1968 comeback masterpiece, produced by Jimmy Miller at Olympic Sound Studios in London.
The music started life as a different song, 'Did Everybody Pay Their Dues?', with the same backing but completely different lyrics about a Native American chief and his family.
Jagger rewrote it after attending the big anti-Vietnam War demonstration at Grosvenor Square in London in March 1968, where protesters clashed with police.
The famous crunch is a trick: Richards played acoustic guitar hard into a Philips cassette recorder with no limiters, overloading it until the acoustic distorted like an electric.
Richards later summed it up: 'Street Fighting Man' was all acoustics — there are no electric guitar parts in it. The only electric instrument on the track is his own bass.
Charlie Watts did not use his normal kit: he played a 1930s toy drum kit, a London Jazz Kit Set he had bought in an antiques shop, run through the same cassette setup.
Brian Jones adds the twanging sitar and tamboura, Traffic's Dave Mason plays shehnai and bass drum, and Nicky Hopkins is on piano.
The lyric even tips its hat to Martha and the Vandellas: 'summer's here and the time is right for fighting in the street' rewrites their 'Dancing in the Street.'

Released as a US single in August 1968, days around the violence at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, many stations — especially in Chicago — refused to play it as subversive. Jagger replied: 'Of course it's subversive!'

Partly because of that radio freeze, it stalled at No. 48 on the Billboard Hot 100; a UK single release did not come until 1971, when it reached No. 21. Rolling Stone has placed it on its 500 Greatest Songs list.

title: Stop-Go
description: One of the oldest Panic originals of all, from the Athens band's debut Space Wrangler — a rolling John Bell tune the faithful also know by its nickname, 'Bookends.'

pops.text: Track seven on Space Wrangler, Widespread Panic's debut studio album, first released February 4, 1988 by the small Atlanta label Landslide Records.
Fans also know the song as 'Bookends' — it is one of the very oldest original songs in the band's repertoire.
JamBase dates its live debut to April 7, 1986, just two months after the band's first official show, and it has been a live staple ever since.
Panic grew it on the Athens club circuit, including a long run of Monday nights at the Uptown Lounge, where 'Stop-Go' joined the batch of early originals alongside 'Porch Song' and 'Driving Song.'
The album was recorded in September 1987 at John Keane's studio in Athens, Georgia. Keane engineered and co-produced it with the band, and became their lifelong collaborator.
The Space Wrangler sessions were a hometown affair, with guests from the Athens scene including fiddle player David Blackmon and keyboard player Tim White across the album.

At 4:50, the studio 'Stop-Go' is compact compared with the live versions, which stretch out — a 2002 Raleigh performance the band later shared officially runs long, with Keane sitting in on pedal steel.
Space Wrangler was cut for vinyl, and space was tight: concert staple 'Conrad,' recorded for the album, was left off the original issue for time.
Writing on the album is credited to the band collectively — John Bell, Michael Houser, Todd Nance, Domingo 'Sunny' Ortiz and Dave Schools on the original tracks.
Later reissues carried the album to Capricorn and then Volcano, whose upload this is. That little 1988 debut inaugurated years of constant touring that made Panic a Southern live institution.

title: Queen Jane Approximately
description: Bob Dylan's 1965 put-down, sung by Bob Weir — this official live cut catches the Dead at Pittsburgh's Civic Arena on April 2, 1989, deep in their Dylan-cover years.

pops.text: The song is Bob Dylan's: he released it in 1965 on Highway 61 Revisited, the album that also carried 'Like a Rolling Stone' and 'Ballad of a Thin Man.'
Dylan also put it out as the B-side of his 1966 single 'One of Us Must Know (Sooner or Later).'
The 'Queen Jane' of the lyric is a figure of Dylan put-down poetry — when all the flower ladies, clowns and authorities have worn the singer out, she is the one he asks to come see him.
The Dead first played it with Dylan himself, on July 4, 1987 at Foxboro, during the joint Dylan & the Dead tour, then kept it for themselves from that September.
In the Dead, it was Bob Weir's song: dead.net notes he sang it frequently with the band from 1987 to 1995, following Dylan's arrangement closely.
This recording comes from April 2, 1989 at the Civic Arena in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania — prime late-eighties Dead, with Brent Mydland on keyboards.
It was officially released on Download Series Vol. 9, which pairs the Pittsburgh shows of April 2 and 3, 1989, and this upload comes from Grateful Dead/Rhino.
Weir also selected the Dead's Dylan performances for the 2002 collection Postcards of the Hanging, which includes a 'Queen Jane Approximately' recorded December 29, 1988.
Dylan covers were a whole second songbook for the Dead: 'Queen Jane' arrived alongside tunes like 'Stuck Inside of Mobile,' 'Maggie's Farm' and 'Ballad of a Thin Man' in the 1987 harvest.
It stayed in rotation to the end — the Dead were still playing it in their final touring year, 1995, nearly thirty years after Dylan wrote it.

title: Friend Like Me
description: Robin Williams' Genie explodes out of the lamp in Alan Menken and Howard Ashman's Cab Calloway-style showstopper — the number that introduced a friend like no other.

pops.text: From Disney's Aladdin, released in 1992, with music by Alan Menken and lyrics by Howard Ashman — the team behind The Little Mermaid and Beauty and the Beast.
Ashman had pitched Aladdin itself to Disney back in 1988. Story changes cut most of his original songs, but 'Friend Like Me,' 'Prince Ali' and 'Arabian Nights' survived into the film.
It began as a Cab Calloway-style big-band number — you can still hear it when the Genie scats — and was then expanded into a pop-culture comedy vehicle once Robin Williams was cast.
In the film, a skeptical Aladdin doubts the Genie's powers, so the Genie answers with this: a full musical sales pitch proving he can be a friend unlike any other.
This was the first scene of Aladdin to have its animation finished, which is why sharp-eyed fans can spot early character-design differences in it.
Genie animator Eric Goldberg's team had the unique job of keeping up with Williams, whose improvisational energy reshaped how animated characters were voiced and drawn.
Sadly, Howard Ashman died in March 1991, before the film was finished, and never saw the number on screen.

The song was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song at the 1993 Oscars — Ashman's last nomination. It lost to the film's other nominee, 'A Whole New World,' and Menken won Best Score for the film.
At just about two and a half minutes on the soundtrack, it is pure density: impressions, transformations, a chorus of thieves, fireworks and a big-band finale, all inside one sales pitch.

Its afterlife keeps growing: Ne-Yo covered it for the 2015 We Love Disney album, Will Smith took his own swing at it in the 2019 live-action remake, and the Genie's Broadway performer won a Tony for the stage version.

title: I'll Make a Man Out of You
description: Disney's ultimate training montage: Donny Osmond, as Captain Li Shang's singing voice, drills a hopeless squad — while Mulan quietly out-thinks them all.

pops.text: Written by composer Matthew Wilder and lyricist David Zippel for Disney's Mulan, with the soundtrack released June 2, 1998.
It replaced an earlier song for the same scene, Stephen Schwartz's 'We'll Make a Man of You,' after Schwartz left the project to work on DreamWorks' The Prince of Egypt.
Wilder and Zippel built the replacement around its ironic title — and Disney approved the first draft right away.
Donny Osmond sings for Captain Li Shang because his singing voice closely matched BD Wong's speaking voice. Osmond studied Wong's dialogue tapes to copy his inflections.
The job was a second chance: Osmond had auditioned to voice Hercules in Disney's previous film and was turned down because the directors thought he sounded too old.
He even sold the pain physically: when Shang takes a hit to the stomach mid-song, Osmond reportedly punched himself in the stomach while recording to make it sound real.

The supporting voices are a family affair: Lea Salonga sings Mulan's line, Harvey Fierstein, Jerry Tondo and co-writer Matthew Wilder himself sing Yao, Chien-Po and Ling, and Eddie Murphy's Mushu gets the scene's one spoken line.

In the film it scores the boot-camp montage, as the hopeless recruits fail at archery, balance and combat — until Mulan, disguised as Ping, solves the impossible pole climb by using the training weights themselves.
That is the song's irony in action: for all its talk of making men, the recruit who masters training is the woman using intelligence instead of brute force.

Osmond still owns it: he sang it with his grandchildren for ABC's 2020 Disney Family Singalong and performs it in his Las Vegas show, while Jackie Chan recorded the song's Mandarin and Cantonese versions. The 2020 remake dropped the singing but still quotes its most famous line.

title: Ziggy Stardust
description: The centrepiece of Bowie's glam-rock masterpiece, telling the birth-to-death story of a bisexual alien rock star in three minutes. This official video stitches Mick Rock's 1972-73 tour footage to the original album recording.

pops.text: Bowie wrote this song and 'Lady Stardust' within days of each other in early 1971, before the Hunky Dory sessions had even begun.
The name was a collage: 'Ziggy' came from a tailor's shop Bowie passed on a train, and 'Stardust' was borrowed from the Legendary Stardust Cowboy.
Another blueprint was English rocker Vince Taylor, who after a breakdown believed he was a cross between a god and an alien — Bowie's 'leper messiah'.
It was recorded on 11 November 1971 at Trident Studios in London, co-produced by Bowie and Ken Scott.
The band is the Spiders from Mars: Mick Ronson on electric guitar, Trevor Bolder on bass and Mick Woodmansey on drums, with Bowie underneath on 12-string acoustic.
That instantly recognisable riff is Ronson's, built around tonic and dominant chords with a hammered fourth — and a second, Byrds-like jangle riff is buried in the mix.
The song opens and closes on the same defining line, 'Ziggy played guitar' — the whole rise and fall of the star is packed in between.
Ziggy plays left-handed in the lyric, one of several nods to Jimi Hendrix woven into the character alongside Iggy Pop and Lou Reed.
Surprise: Bowie's original was never released as a single. A live version only became a single in France in 1994, to promote Santa Monica '72.
Rolling Stone placed it at No. 282 on its 2010 list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time, and Bauhaus took their 1982 cover of it to No. 15 in the UK.

title: Put It Where You Want It
description: A five-and-a-half-minute jazz-funk groove from the double album Crusaders 1, driven by Joe Sample's keyboards. No singer, no words — just a riff so catchy it crossed over to the pop charts.

pops.text: No vocals at all: this is a pure instrumental, written by keyboard player Joe Sample, the band's musical engine.
The group had just shortened its name. After a decade as the Jazz Crusaders, they dropped the 'Jazz' in 1971 and leaned fully into electric funk.
The core members — Sample, saxophonist Wilton Felder, trombonist Wayne Henderson and drummer Stix Hooper — were Houston high-school friends who first played together as the Swingsters in 1954.
It comes from Crusaders 1, a 1972 double album on Blue Thumb Records produced by Stewart Levine, recorded at Wally Heider Studios in Hollywood.
The album was a statement of intent: AllMusic called the reinvention a wonder of jazz-funk evolving naturally out of hard bop and soul-jazz.
Listen for the guests: solo guitarist Larry Carlton, guitarists Arthur Adams and David T. Walker, and electric bassist Chuck Rainey all play on the album.
Crusaders 1 peaked at No. 3 on Billboard's Top Jazz LPs chart, and earned a Grammy nomination for Best R&B Instrumental Performance.
As a single, this track reached No. 52 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1972 — a real crossover result for a jazz instrumental — and No. 39 on the R&B chart.
The album version runs about 5:30, roughly twice as long as the edited single version sold on 45.
Its afterlife started fast: the Average White Band covered it in 1973, and it has remained the track that represents this era on Crusaders best-of collections.

title: Layla
description: Eric Clapton's desperate love song in two movements — a screaming guitar first half and a long, dreamy piano coda. The full album version, with Duane Allman's slide guitar all over it.

pops.text: The title comes from Nizami Ganjavi's 12th-century Persian poem The Story of Layla and Majnun, about a young man driven mad by unrequited love — a copy was given to Clapton.
The real-life Layla was Pattie Boyd, wife of Clapton's close friend George Harrison. Clapton was desperately in love with her when he wrote it.
Clapton first wrote it as a ballad. It became a rocker when Duane Allman, who joined the sessions as a guest, came up with the signature riff, according to Clapton.
Producer Tom Dowd introduced Clapton and Allman at an Allman Brothers concert in Miami on 26 August 1970; Dowd described their guitar chemistry as telepathy.
It was recorded at Criteria Studios in Miami. The first section alone stacks six guitar tracks, with Clapton and Allman doubling the famous seven-note riff.
Both guitarists plugged into the same two-input Fender Champ amplifier for parts of the recording — a tiny amp behind a huge sound.

The second half is a different song entirely: drummer Jim Gordon's piano piece, which Clapton heard in the studio and persuaded him to attach. It was recorded about a week later and spliced on by Dowd.
In the coda, Allman pushes his slide beyond the end of the fretboard to hit what Dowd called 'notes that aren't on the instrument', ending on his high 'bird call'.
Radio resisted its length at first: a 2:43 edit peaked at only No. 51 in the US in 1971. The full version, re-released in 1972, reached No. 10 in the US and No. 7 in the UK.
Rolling Stone ranked it No. 27 on its 500 Greatest Songs of All Time in 2004, and Clapton's acoustic Unplugged remake won the 1993 Grammy for Best Rock Song.

title: The Goonies 'R' Good Enough
description: Cyndi Lauper's synth-pop theme for The Goonies, with a two-part mini-movie video full of wrestlers, pirates and the Goonies kids themselves. Pure 1985: treasure map, gas station and André the Giant.

pops.text: It began life simply as 'Good Enough', written in 1984 by Lauper with Stephen Broughton Lunt and Arthur Stead. Warner Bros. added 'The Goonies 'R'' to the title for marketing.
Executive producer Steven Spielberg made Lauper the musical director of The Goonies soundtrack — she brought in her friends the Bangles for the album, too.
Lauper has admitted she hated the song, and she refused to play it live after 1987. Fan demand finally coaxed it back into her set in Australia in 2004.
Released on 6 June 1985, a day before the film opened, it peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 on 13 July 1985 — her fifth top-ten single.
It also made the top ten in Australia and Canada, but it never entered the UK Singles Chart at all, which makes British pressings rare for collectors.
The video was directed by the film's own director, Richard Donner, and shot as a two-part adventure: Part 1 hit MTV on 7 May 1985, Part 2 after the film opened.
The creditors trying to evict Cyndi's family are WWF wrestlers: Roddy Piper, Freddie Blassie, the Iron Sheik and Nikolai Volkoff, with Captain Lou Albano as her dad.
Spot the cameos: most of the young Goonies cast, the Bangles as female pirates, Lauper's mother as a sea hag — and Spielberg himself, in an editing room, unable to help Cyndi out of a cliffhanger.
André the Giant appears only in Part 2, arriving in a cloud of smoke to chase the creditors away.
Part 1 nearly vanished: Warner Bros. could not find its master tape for the Goonies DVD until someone at VH1 found an unused broadcast copy just in time to digitise it.

title: Shine
description: The demo that refused to stay a demo: Ed Roland's droning riff and 'heaven let your light shine down' chorus became 1994's biggest album-rock song. The video mixes black-and-white rural footage with the band in a shed.

pops.text: Ed Roland wrote it in about one sitting in his parents' living room, jamming with his younger brother Dean — who he had not even known played guitar. He dates the song to about 1989.
Roland called the style 'drone': hold an A or an E underneath and play a melody over it. The 'Shine' riff was the one he kept coming back to.
That famous 'yeah' before the chorus? Roland has said he sang it through an empty toilet-paper roll he found in his bathroom.
The song first appeared on Hints Allegations and Things Left Unsaid in 1993, a collection built around Roland's demos, before Atlantic gave it a full push as a single in 1994.
College radio broke it: an Atlanta station took a chance on the demo, it became a regional smash, and Atlantic signed the band in January 1994.

Because the lyric mentions heaven, the band were repeatedly labelled a Christian band. Roland pushed back, noting Led Zeppelin sang about heaven too; his father was a Southern Baptist minister, but he said no single doctrine spoke for the band.
Dean Roland has called the chorus 'basically a prayer' — an uplifting song that stood out in the middle of the grunge years.
Chart peak: No. 1 on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks for eight weeks, and the chart's No. 1 song of 1994, plus No. 11 on the Hot 100 and No. 4 on Modern Rock Tracks.
The video, directed by William Levin, is largely black-and-white: kids haul random objects across fields and railroad tracks to an old shed where the band is playing. It became an MTV staple.
Dolly Parton covered it bluegrass-style, with members of Nickel Creek, on her 2001 album Little Sparrow — and won the Grammy for Best Female Country Vocal Performance for it.

title: Our Day Will Come
description: A dreamy bossa-nova promise from an Akron vocal group on their very first recording, topped by a swirling Hammond organ solo. It went all the way to No. 1 in the spring of 1963.

pops.text: The group were from Akron, Ohio: lead singer Ruby Nash with Ed Roberts, George Lee, Ronald Mosely and Leroy Fann. Kapp Records renamed them Ruby and the Romantics.
Songwriters Mort Garson and Bob Hilliard wrote it hoping to place it with an established easy-listening singer — crooner Jack Jones was the intended voice.
The group talked their way into it: Kapp's Allen Stanton only got the writers' permission by promising that if this version failed, Jack Jones would record it next.
Stanton cut two versions — a mid-tempo ballad and a bossa nova arrangement. The bossa nova take, with its Hammond organ solo, is the one that was released.
That organ solo is played by Leroy Glover, and the session band also included jazz guitarist Kenny Burrell, plus Vinnie Bell and Al Gorgoni on guitars.
Released as a single in December 1962, it climbed for weeks and reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the week of 23 March 1963.
It was a double No. 1, topping the Billboard R&B chart as well, and it sold over a million copies in the US — all from the group's first recording.
It earned the group a Grammy nomination for Best Rock and Roll Recording at the 1964 awards — an early sign of how loose that category could be.
Around the world it reached No. 1 in New Zealand and No. 11 in Australia, though it stopped at No. 38 in the UK.
Everyone wanted a turn afterwards: Frankie Valli took it back to No. 11 in 1975, and Amy Winehouse's version was released posthumously in 2011.

title: Better Things
description: Ray Davies turns a divorce into a blessing: a three-minute wish for blue skies and better choruses that closes Give the People What They Want on a note of pure hope.

pops.text: Ray Davies wrote it in New York City about the impending split from his second wife, Yvonne — he called that period a depressing time.
It is a breakup song with no bitterness: Davies wishes his ex the bluest sky and hopes all her verses rhyme — wishing her well on the way out.
The song dates to 1979 and the Low Budget sessions, where an early version was attempted — and turned down, Davies said, because the band could not get it together.
It was finally recorded in April 1981 at Konk Studios in London for Give the People What They Want, in a session Davies dubbed 'a total send-up'.
Davies heard it as classic Kinks, like 'Days': a melody climbing the scale, with a harmonic swerve — F sharp major where you expect B7 — that he called a musical trick.
He sequenced it as the album's closer on purpose, saying after a song like 'A Little Bit of Abuse' you need some hope — and that this song gave him hope.
Released as a UK single on 19 June 1981, early copies came with a bonus 7-inch of live 'Lola' and 'David Watts' recorded on American tours.
Its chart numbers were modest — No. 46 in the UK and No. 92 on the Hot 100, though No. 12 on Billboard's Rock Top Tracks — but No. 46 mattered: it was the Kinks' first UK chart single since 1972.
In 2011 American Songwriter named it their Favorite Breakup Song.

Its second life is remarkable: Fountains of Wayne sang it on late-night TV ten days after 9/11, Pearl Jam issued it as a 2011 fan-club single, and Bruce Springsteen duetted on it with Davies on the 2010 album See My Friends.
